subject: Computer Networking
title: Free-Space Optical Communication
description: A 60-second lesson on Free-Space Optical Communication.

hook.text: Beam data through air using lasers instead of radio. Free-space optical links already do this.

buildup.text: FSO uses focused lasers to transmit data point-to-point. No fiber — just line of sight.

discovery.text: FSO hits 10+ Gbps over kilometers. Used for building links and satellite crosslinks in space.

twist.text: Fog, rain, and dust scatter the beam. Atmosphere limits reliability. Adaptive optics help.

climax.text: Starlink uses laser crosslinks between satellites — no atmosphere to interfere. Light speed data.

punchline.text: FSO: fiber speed, no fiber needed. Perfect in space, tricky on Earth.

quiz.question: What is the main challenge of free-space optical communication on Earth?
options: Weather conditions like fog and rain scatter the laser beam
The lasers are too expensive to manufacture
The speed is much slower than radio communication

details.summary: Free-space optical communication uses laser beams to transmit data through the atmosphere between fixed points. It provides fiber-like speeds of 10 Gbps or more without physical cables, making it ideal for connecting buildings, temporary sites, and areas where laying fiber is impractical.
details.whyItMatters: FSO offers the bandwidth of fiber optics where fiber cannot be installed. It provides rapid deployment for enterprise, military, and disaster recovery communication links.
takeaways: Laser beams carry data through the atmosphere at fiber speeds
No physical cables or spectrum licenses are needed
Weather conditions like fog and rain can degrade performance

faq.question: How does weather affect free-space optical communication?
faq.answer: Fog is the biggest challenge because water droplets scatter light. Heavy rain and snow also degrade signal quality. Most deployments use hybrid FSO/RF systems that fall back to microwave radio during poor visibility.

faq.question: What distances can FSO links cover?
faq.answer: Terrestrial FSO links typically span 200 meters to 5 kilometers depending on weather conditions. Some high-power systems reach 10 kilometers in clear conditions. In space, laser communication between satellites covers thousands of kilometers because there is no atmosphere to interfere.
